title: I shipped my first game in ~3 weeks of evenings with Claude Code – Godot 4, Android + PC
author: Naive-Hornet2237
selftext:
Yesterday I released Luxaplex: Restore Point, a grid-based puzzle game (31 levels, 5 worlds, a boss, a level editor) on Google Play and itch.io. I'm a solo hobby dev with a day job, and I built it with Claude Code as my coding partner. Some notes on how that worked:

What I did: the idea and design, world themes and mechanics, choosing and tuning levels, playtesting on my phone, every decision about scope, store pages and release.

What the AI did: most of the GDScript, a test suite (mechanics tests + a BFS bot that proves every level is solvable, screen-flow and translation tests), a level generator I picked levels from, pixel art drawn by Python scripts, synthesized music and SFX, the GitHub Actions pipeline that builds the Android AAB with AdMob + Play Billing, and help with store listings and the privacy policy.

What worked well:

• "Plan first, then code" – I approve the scope of every version before anything is written.

• Every iteration is a version with a CHANGELOG, and all tests must pass before it ships.

• Automated tests caught a lot – the bot replays every level after each change.

• An external audit (I asked ChatGPT to review the build) found real bugs before launch.

What didn't:

• The AI can't feel if something is fun or readable on a small screen – that's still your job.

• Platform stuff (Play Console, AdMob consent, payments) needs a human clicking through a lot of screens.

Android (free): https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=eu.luxier.luxaplex

PC (pay what you want): https://luxiergames.itch.io/luxaplex-restore-point

Happy to answer questions about the workflow!

comments.author: moeinh77
comments.body: cool thanks for sharing. i wonder how easy was the graphics and pixel art with ai + python. did it get it easily?

replies.author: Naive-Hornet2237
replies.body:
Thanks! Honestly – it was surprisingly easy, maybe too easy.
There's no image generator involved. The AI wrote Python scripts (Pillow) that draw every sprite pixel by pixel: 32×32 tiles, a fixed palette, simple shapes and shading rules, then pack everything into one atlas for Godot. Each world's tiles (RAM, HDD, GPU, CPU, BIOS) come from their own script, so changing a color or a detail is just editing a few lines and re-running it.
My part was art direction and lots of iteration: "this wall looks too much like the blinking wall on the GPU level", "the hero needs more glow", "this doesn't read on a small phone screen" – and so on, many rounds until it looked right.
Because it was that easy, for my next games I'm drawing my own sprites, so not everything comes from AI. Still, I think it turned out pretty well here – it doesn't look as generic as a lot of AI-made games, mostly thanks to the consistent palette and all that back-and-forth.
